# Draft:Treaty of Cuba

The Treaty of Cuba, signed on March 7, 1848 on the Island of Cuba in Lake Nicaragua was an agreement between the Kingdom of Mosquitia, a British-protected indigenous monarchy on the Caribbean coast of Central America, and the State of Nicaragua. The treaty marked a temporary resolution to the escalating territorial conflict over San Juan del Norte (modern-day Grey Town), a key Atlantic port at the mouth of the River San Juan.[https://hdl.handle.net/2027/uc1.aa0011616547]
Historical Context
The Mosquitian Shore had long been distinct from Spanish-controlled Nicaragua, both politically and culturally. The Miskito and other people of the Shore, supported intermittently by the British Empire, claimed sovereignty over a wide coastal area stretching from River Aguan in the north to the Moskitian Gulf in the south, with Grey Town and the River San Juan lying in the middle. Colonial-era documents—including a 1576 Royal Ordinance of Philip II—confirm that Nicaragua’s jurisdiction did not extend to the River San Juan or the eastern coast.[https://hdl.handle.net/2027/loc.ark:/13960/t41r7ks0s?urlappend=%3Bseq=29]
Even after independence, Nicaragua had not established a lasting presence east of Lake Nicaragua. In fact, the region was historically referred to as part of Veragua or Taguzgalpa, and never formally integrated into Spanish Nicaragua. However, by the early 19th century, Nicaragua began asserting control over the San Juan River and its Caribbean terminus, with officials such as Manuel Quijano, Antonio Salinas, and Rafael Bermúdez posted at Grey Town between 1838 and 1847.[https://hdl.handle.net/2027/mdp.39015086610840]
Rising Tensions and the Moskitian Ultimatum
On October 25, 1847, the Council of State of the Kingdom of Mosquitia, backed by Britain, formally demanded that Nicaraguan forces withdraw from Grey Town by January 1, 1848. Nicaragua refused, and in early January, Mosquitian forces reasserted control of the port. Nicaragua retaliated on January 10, 1848, when Lt. Col. Antonio Salas led an armed expedition that arrested two Mosquitian officials, hauled down the Mosquitian flag (which he took with him), but failed to reoccupy the town, instead retreating upriver.
The 1848 San Juan Expedition
In response to Nicaragua's armed incursion and the detention of Mosquitian officials, the British Royal Navy dispatched Captain Granville Gower Loch aboard HMS Alarm to lead an expedition up the San Juan River to obtain redress from Nicaragua and the release of the Mosquitian officials. Loch's forces, which included Royal Marines and local auxiliaries, launched a brief campaign known as the San Juan Expedition of 1848.
Terms of the treaty
Under the terms of the treaty Nicaragua agreed to withdraw from the contested territories, including Grey Town; Mosquitia retained de facto control of the port-town and surrounding coast; and the parties would pursue diplomatic means to resolve the territorial dispute.
The treaty was primarily a ceasefire and recognition of the status quo, not a permanent settlement of sovereignty.
